article_content: Chinese tennis star Li Na credits her grueling preseason workouts for securing a spot in the Australian Open semifinals, marking her third appearance since 2011. The sixth-seeded athlete triumphed over Poland's fourth-ranked Agnieszka Radwanska (7-5, 6-3) in a 102-minute match, advancing to her first major semifinal since making history as Asia's inaugural Grand Slam singles winner at the 2011 French Open. Since partnering with Carlos Rodriguez - former mentor to seven-time major champion Justine Henin - last year, Li's regimen now combines intense court sessions with exhaustive fitness training. 'We train 5-6 hours daily, split between tennis drills and physical conditioning,' the 30-year-old explained after securing a semifinal clash with world No. 2 Maria Sharapova. 'After three days with Carlos, I told my husband Jiang Shan he must be crazy!' The coaching switch from her spouse sparked unfounded divorce rumors, which Li addressed humorously: 'Two years back, people asked if we'd split! Working with a life partner as coach created tension - we'd argue about training demands. But Jiang supported this professional change.' Li's enhanced stamina proved crucial against Radwanska, who'd previously beaten her in Sydney. 'She forces you to maintain absolute focus,' Li noted about the grueling encounter. 'Any weak shot becomes an instant attack opportunity.' Sharapova enters the semifinal with dominant form, having conceded only nine games total. The 2008 champion dismissed concerns about easy matches affecting readiness: 'My goal isn't to be tested - it's to win efficiently. If challenges arise, I'll adapt.' Despite pre-tournament injury concerns, the Russian has earned $1,587 per minute of court time across her five straight-set victories.

article_content: Watches of Switzerland's shares surged 9.8% to 570p following improved quarterly results and a bold growth strategy reveal. The FTSE 250 constituent reported a 5% constant-currency revenue increase to £379 million for the 13 weeks ending October 29, with U.S. sales jumping 11% on this basis to £165 million. While maintaining full-year guidance of 8-11% growth, the company acknowledged challenges from August's  share price dip after Rolex's Bucherer acquisition. CEO Brian Duffy emphasized their 'proven model' continues delivering results, with luxury watches (87% of sales) seeing 3% underlying growth despite flat reported figures. A five-year £350-500 million investment plan aims to double sales to £3 billion by FY2028 through showroom expansions and pre-owned market pushes - including expectations that refurbished Rolexes will account for 20% of U.S. sales through the brand's certified program.

article_content: Emerging studies suggest middle names might offer unexpected professional advantages. Research demonstrates that individuals displaying middle initials are perceived as more competent, particularly in academic and legal fields. In controlled experiments, authors using middle initials received higher credibility ratings for identical work – with David F. Clark's paper scoring better than David Clark's, though excessive initials (like David F.P.R. Clark) showed diminishing returns. The 'initial effect' complements name pronunciation research from UC Irvine, where simpler names inspired greater trust. Practical implications emerge in team selection: participants preferred quiz teams with middle-initialized members, though this preference disappeared for athletic teams. Psychologists attribute this to cultural associations with high-status professions where multi-part names are common. While parents might view multiple middle names as educational investments, experts note that lasting success still requires genuine capability. The studies highlight how superficial cues interact with professional perceptions in complex ways.
